newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: Efforts to resolve East Timor bearing little fruit.
newsitem.headline: Efforts to resolve East Timor bearing little fruit.

text.p: International pressure has mounted on Indonesia in the past week to resolve the tension and bitterness in East Timor, but there are few signs in the troubled territory that the situation is headed for change.

In the past seven days, the Vatican, the United Nations and the United States have called for a speedy settlement to one of the world's longest running and thorniest political issues -- the future of the former Portuguese colony of East Timor.

The Vatican installed a bishop last week in the newly- created diocese of Baucau in the Roman Catholic-dominated territory, enhancing the role of the church as a peace broker in Indonesia's suppression of a movement for self-determination.
Indonesia invaded the territory in 1975 and annexed it the following year.
Pope John Paul said in a message that the people of East Timor "await a response to their legitimate aspirations for the recognition of their specific cultural and religious identity".
He hoped "a broad and truly just internationally accepted solution will be found to the complex and painful question...."

Jamsheed Marker, the recently-appointed U.N. special envoy for East Timor, visited the territory for the first time at the weekend, and said he believed there was "a desire and, God willing, a possibility (for a solution)".
U.N.-sponsored talks between Portugal, which is demanding self-determination for the East Timorese, and Indonesia have been deadlocked for nearly 15 years.

Marker's visit followed a tour by U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck, who said his 24-hour stopover left him "with a sense of hope...that the discussion of human rights and the future of East Timor can proceed to a new level".
But the high-level visits and the hopes expressed by the diplomats had little effect on East Timor's most influential leader, Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Bishop Carlos Belo.
"I am here already 14 years. I hear the same things, the same resolutions," he told Reuters in an interview. "We hope that with these visitors something will change. But I am not hopeful."
On Monday, Belo said in a statement to the U.N. Human Rights Commission that Indonesian security forces routinely tortured East Timorese prisoners, many held on political charges.
"In the name of all Timorese prisoners, persecuted youth and oppressed families, I wish to make a plea for greater respect of human dignity in East Timor," he said.

On the surface, East Timor shows little sign of oppression. The capital Dili is a picturesque bungalow-dotted town nestled on a plain between the clear-blue waters of Dili Bay and the bleak forested hills to the south.
There are few signs of the estimated 7,000 to 10,000 troops on the island and even the police presence is muted.

But dissidence is quickly snuffed out. When a group of students demonstrated against Indonesian rule on Sunday at the Dili hotel where Marker was staying, police swiftly broke up the protest and arrested 48 people. Eleven were injured. Residents and human rights groups estimate about 200,000 to 250,000 people died in East Timor since Indonesia's 1975 invasion, a subsequent famine and two decades of strife.
"The tensions are because of the imposition of a military solution to a political problem," said Florentino Sarmento, who heads an agricultural development programme from Dili.
"For 20 years, Indonesia has not succeeded in finding a political solution."
He said in the past two decades, Indonesia had achieved significant advances in economic development and stature in international relations. "But East Timor is still there."
Official Indonesian sources have said the integration of East Timor into the country is an accomplished fact and President Suharto has rejected "autonomy" for the territory.
The sources said a way around this may be found, however, by granting East Timor "special region" status, which has historical precedent elsewhere in the country.

A diplomat who has closely followed recent events in East Timor said there was a possibility of some movement on resolving the issue given the international pressure on Indonesia and on Portugal, but overall he was cautious.

"The convergence of events is encouraging," he told Reuters. "But if looked at closely, it is difficult to envision progress. It is difficult to see progress on East Timor outside of a transition in Indonesia itself."
